title: One table, different rows: query-time row access policies
goal: Filter rows by the caller's identity without making a separate table per team.
concept:
A hotel clerk may open the same booking system as a regional manager, but should see fewer rooms. The table does not change; the visible result changes with the caller.

A row policy is a predicate evaluated at query time. It does not grant table access by itself. First the caller needs ordinary object privileges; then the policy removes rows that are outside that caller's allowed region.
example: The table contains orders east-42, west-77, and east-99. The group east_analysts receives two east rows. west_analysts receives one west row. A governance administrator may receive all three. The physical rows are unchanged.

use_case.when: Use row-level policy when many users query the same governed table but each user or role may see only a subset of rows.
use_case.example: Regional finance teams share one orders table; east analysts must never receive west customer records.
use_case.decision: Choose a centralized policy when the rule repeats across many tables; use a table-level rule for narrow table-specific logic. Prefer separate datasets when legal or operational isolation requires a stronger physical boundary.

practice: Switch the active identity. Predict which order cards survive the policy before revealing the result.
boundary: The browser filters three synthetic rows locally. It does not execute Unity Catalog or Snowflake, prove that identity groups are configured correctly, model policy-owner privileges, prevent inference through every query, or measure policy cost. Vendor SQL is sourced but not executed.

').join('')+'

Visible rows: '+policyRows.filter(r=>who==='admin'||r[1]===who).map(r=>r[0]).join(', ')+'

';};policyCaller.onchange=paintPolicy;paintPolicy();

product_sections.title: Databricks: Unity Catalog row filter UDF
product_sections.html:
Mechanism. A SQL UDF returns true for rows the caller may see. Attach it with ALTER TABLE ... SET ROW FILTER. Databricks recommends ABAC policies when the same rule must scale across many tagged tables.

-- sourced pattern; not executed hereCREATE FUNCTION governance.region_filter(region STRING)RETURN is_account_group_member('governance_admin')   OR is_account_group_member(concat(region, '_analysts'));ALTER TABLE sales.ordersSET ROW FILTER governance.region_filter ON (region);

Failure/fix. A per-table filter can be missed on a newly created table. For broad repeatable governance, use tagged ABAC policies and test policy coverage. The filter is an added restriction; base privileges are still required.

Boundary. Unity Catalog is required. UDF complexity and secure evaluation can affect optimization. This lesson does not run the SQL.
product_sections.markdown: Databricks uses a row-filter UDF attached to a Unity Catalog table. Rows for which the function returns false are excluded. Prefer ABAC for repeatable tag-driven coverage across many tables. SQL is unexecuted.

product_sections.title: Snowflake: schema-level row access policy
product_sections.html:
Mechanism. A row access policy is a schema object whose boolean expression is evaluated at query time. Attach it to one or more tables or views. Snowflake evaluates its expression using the policy owner's role, enabling protected mapping-table lookups.

-- sourced pattern; not executed hereCREATE ROW ACCESS POLICY governance.region_policyAS (region STRING) RETURNS BOOLEAN ->  CURRENT_ROLE() = 'GOVERNANCE_ADMIN'  OR EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM governance.role_region             WHERE role_name = CURRENT_ROLE()               AND allowed_region = region);ALTER TABLE sales.orders ADD ROW ACCESS POLICY  governance.region_policy ON (region);

Failure/fix. A row access policy controls visibility; it does not stop inserts or changes to rows a role can already modify. Grant DML separately and test that policy context, ownership, and mapping rows are correct.

Boundary. Row access policies are an Enterprise Edition feature. Policy evaluation and mapping-table design have privilege and performance implications. This lesson does not run the SQL.
product_sections.markdown: Snowflake row access policies are reusable schema objects attached to tables or views. Their boolean expression controls which rows appear at query time. They do not independently block inserts or grant object privileges. SQL is unexecuted.

title: Readers keep a snapshot; writers pay for a copy
goal: Use CopyOnWriteArrayList only when reads vastly outnumber writes.
concept:
A museum prints a visitor map each morning. Visitors can keep reading that map even while staff prepare tomorrow's version. Readers never see half-edited ink; the staff pays the cost of printing a new map.

CopyOnWriteArrayList works that way. A mutation copies the backing array. An iterator keeps the array reference it captured, so later additions do not appear in that iterator.
example: A listener list starts as [billing, audit]. Request A creates an iterator. Another thread adds fraud, producing a new array. Request A still calls only billing and audit. A new request sees all three listeners.

use_case.when: Use it for small listener, route, or configuration lists that are traversed constantly and changed rarely.
use_case.example: A Java service invokes two event listeners on every Kafka record but updates the listener set only during a rare configuration change.
use_case.decision: Choose it when traversal dominates and stale snapshot iteration is acceptable. Use another concurrent structure or explicit immutable snapshot publication when writes, list size, or freshness requirements make copying expensive.

practice: Create an iterator, then add a listener. Compare the old iterator's snapshot with a newly created iterator.
boundary: The browser models array identities and snapshot visibility. The Java replay runs single-threaded. Neither measures allocation, contention, GC cost, or timing, and it does not prove correctness for mutable elements stored inside the list.

function paintCow(){const add=addListener.checked;cowWorld.innerHTML='
iterator snapshot · array A
billing · audit
current list · '+(add?'array B':'array A')+'
billing · audit'+(add?' · fraud':'')+'

Old iterator sees 2; new iterator sees '+(add?3:2)+'.

';};addListener.onchange=paintCow;paintCow();
questions: An iterator exists before fraud is added. What does it see?
Only billing and audit
All three listeners
A ConcurrentModificationException
The iterator keeps its creation-time array snapshot.
Why can traversal avoid synchronization?
The captured array is not mutated
All writes are ignored
Elements become immutable
Writers publish a fresh backing array.
When is this structure a poor fit?
Large or frequently mutated lists
Tiny read-mostly lists
Snapshot-tolerant listener registries
Every mutation copies the backing array.

steps.note: Create the read-mostly listener list.
The iterator captures the current backing-array snapshot.
The write publishes a copied array containing three values.

steps.code: var currentCount = listeners.size(); var oldCount = 0; while (oldIterator.hasNext()) { oldIterator.next(); oldCount++; }
steps.note: The current list has three values while the old snapshot still has two.

title: Put toil on a budget before it owns the roadmap
goal: Turn recurring operational work into a visible capacity decision.
concept:
A team has a 40-hour jar. Every manual replay, access fix, and release ticket takes time from the same jar as reliability engineering. If recurring work grows quietly, roadmap misses look like an execution problem instead of a capacity fact.

Google SRE defines toil as work that is manual, repetitive, automatable, tactical, lacks enduring value, or grows linearly with the service. The leadership move is to measure it, cap it, and fund work that removes the largest recurring source.
example: A six-person platform group spends 108 hours each week on manual tenant onboarding: 45% of its 240-hour capacity. A 30% local toil budget allows 72 hours. The 36-hour overflow is explicit. Automating onboarding by 24 hours still leaves a 12-hour gap; leaders must remove more toil, reduce commitments, or add sustainable capacity.

use_case.when: Use a toil budget when repeated operational work keeps displacing platform improvements or grows with tenants, pipelines, or services.
use_case.example: Every new data domain requires four manual IAM, catalog, and topic tickets, so onboarding work scales linearly with adoption.
use_case.decision: Classify work by its attributes, measure hands-on time, set a local target, and rank elimination projects by recurring hours removed and risk. Do not label necessary novel incident learning as toil just because it is unpleasant.

practice: Move weekly toil hours. Watch which roadmap capacity disappears and when the chosen budget is exceeded.
boundary: This is a capacity arithmetic model, not a universal staffing prescription. Google's published 50% SRE goal is context, not a mandated target for every team. The model ignores interrupt variance, skill mix, on-call recovery, and project dependencies.

';};toilHours.oninput=paintToil;paintToil();

title: Hand off only the context the next agent needs
goal: Filter agent handoff history without pretending it is an authorization boundary.
concept:
A hospital referral should carry the diagnosis and relevant tests, not every hallway conversation. An agent handoff has the same design choice: the next specialist can receive the full conversation, or a filtered version.

In the OpenAI Agents SDK, a handoff input filter transforms HandoffInputData. It can remove tool chatter or summarize prior history. That changes context quality and privacy exposure; it does not grant or revoke tool authority.
example: A triage agent collects an order number, a customer email, two tool results, and a refund reason. The refund specialist needs the order number and reason. The filter drops tool-call plumbing and redacts the email before the handoff. The specialist's tool permissions are configured separately.

use_case.when: Use a handoff filter when a specialist needs a narrower, cleaner, or redacted history than the originating agent accumulated.
use_case.example: A support triage agent delegates a refund decision while keeping payment lookup internals and unrelated conversation out of the specialist context.
use_case.decision: Define the minimum fields needed for the next task, preserve auditability of what was transferred, and test omissions. Use separate tool and authorization controls; context filtering alone is not least privilege.

practice: Toggle full and filtered transfer. Inspect exactly which context items cross the handoff boundary.
boundary: This browser moves synthetic cards. It does not run an agent, summarize with a model, enforce tool permissions, protect server-managed conversations, or prove privacy. Official docs note server-managed conversations do not support handoff input filters through RunConfig.

title: Concentrate phosphate where the reaction happens
goal: Understand a new solid-electrolyte approach to dilute-water phosphate removal.
concept:
Trying to catch a few grains of salt in a swimming pool is slow because the grains rarely reach the catcher. Dilute phosphate remediation has the same mass-transport problem.

A 2026 Nature Communications paper reports a solid-state electrolyte electrocoagulation system. Its interface enriches phosphate locally, then an anodic reaction forms coagulants at that same place. The research claim is that local concentration and improved ion transport accelerate removal in low-conductivity water.
example: In a teaching model, 100 phosphate units are spread through a large volume. A conventional surface receives 10 units per interval. An enrichment interface receives 35, so more phosphate is available where coagulation occurs. The paper reports 0.197 mg/L·min removal, 0.0325 kWh/g P energy, and 3.829 g iron/g P in its evaluated setup.

use_case.when: This is specialist research for decentralized treatment of low-level phosphate in low-conductivity natural water, not a general-purpose production recipe.
use_case.example: The paper validates a photovoltaic-integrated boat-mounted unit intended to treat natural waters below a stated regulatory threshold.
use_case.decision: Treat it as a research claim until site-specific water chemistry, maintenance, lifetime, safety, cost, by-products, scaling, and independent replication are evaluated. Do not transfer headline rates to another water body without testing.

practice: Change interface enrichment. Watch phosphate move from the dilute pool to the reaction surface and compare captured units per interval.
boundary: This is an original mass-transfer teaching model, not the paper's equations, apparatus, dataset, or source-data analysis. It does not model electrochemistry, competing ions, fouling, hydrodynamics, energy, iron dose, or regulatory validation.

title: Block the newly vulnerable dependency, not the whole history
goal: Use dependency review as a pull-request delta gate.
concept:
A building inspector checks the new room added by today's permit, not every brick ever laid. GitHub dependency review compares dependency changes in a pull request and can fail when the change introduces a dependency with a known vulnerability.

The key word is introduced. A pull-request gate helps stop new risk from entering. Existing vulnerable dependencies still need an inventory and remediation program.
example: A pull request upgrades widget-lib from 1.4 to 2.0 and adds parser-x 3.1. The dependency review finds a high-severity advisory on parser-x. With fail-on-severity: high and the job marked required, the merge is blocked. A moderate advisory does not cross that chosen threshold.

use_case.when: Use dependency review on repositories whose pull requests change supported package manifests or lockfiles and where new vulnerable or disallowed dependencies should block merge.
use_case.example: A Java data-service PR adds a serializer library; the required dependency-review job checks the dependency diff before the service can merge.
use_case.decision: Choose a severity and license policy that matches organizational risk, make the check required, and manage exceptions explicitly. Pair it with scanning and remediation for vulnerabilities already present.

practice: Change the highest severity introduced by the PR. Watch the required check pass or block at the configured threshold.
boundary: The browser evaluates four severity labels. It does not call GitHub, parse manifests, query the Advisory Database, model transitive reachability or license policy, or prove that a status check is required. Availability depends on GitHub plan and repository configuration.

title: Wait for ready, but never wait past the deadline
goal: Queue a gRPC call through transient connection failure without making it unbounded.
concept:
An elevator is temporarily between floors. You can leave immediately and take the stairs, or wait—provided you still leave by your appointment time. gRPC's Wait-for-Ready makes the same choice for an RPC created while the channel is in transient failure.

Without it, the call fails immediately. With it, the call waits for the channel to become ready. The deadline still applies and stops the wait.
example: A batch worker creates ReconcileOrder while the channel is in TRANSIENT_FAILURE. The service recovers after 3 seconds. With a 5-second deadline and Wait-for-Ready, the request is sent with 2 seconds remaining. With a 2-second deadline, it ends before recovery.

use_case.when: Use Wait-for-Ready for batch or startup flows where a short transient connection failure should be absorbed and the caller has a meaningful deadline.
use_case.example: A scheduled reconciliation worker starts while the gRPC service is rolling and can wait a few seconds before sending its idempotent request.
use_case.decision: Enable it selectively, always set deadlines, and bound queue/memory pressure. Prefer immediate failure for interactive requests that need fast fallback or when waiting would hide a sustained outage.

practice: Set recovery time and deadline. Watch the RPC remain queued, send with remaining budget, or expire.
boundary: This local state model does not create a gRPC channel, model resolver/load-balancer states, backoff, permanent failures, cancellation races, retries, hedging, queue limits, streaming, or language-specific APIs.
